analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare directly negotiate prescription drug prices with manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees and a health subcommittee and never received a markup, hearing, or vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal a 2003 law that bars Medicare from negotiating drug prices, and instead require the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate prices for the most expensive drugs used by Part D beneficiaries. If talks failed, the Secretary could set the price at the lowest of the Veterans Affairs price, the average price in ten large wealthy countries, or Medicaid's 'best price'. It would also create a national Medicare drug formulary and require drugmakers to pay Medicaid-style rebates on drugs dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees, with the money going back into the Medicare drug account.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Part D beneficiaries — particularly the roughly third of enrollees who are low-income — who would benefit from negotiated prices on the costliest drugs, mandatory rebates on drugs dispensed to low-income enrollees, and an appeal process to get off-formulary drugs covered. Taxpayers also benefit because lower Part D drug spending and rebate deposits reduce federal Medicare outlays.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 'non-interference' provision and requires the Secretary to negotiate prices, discounts, and rebates with drug manufacturers for covered Part D drugs, starting with plan year 2019.

Prioritizes the highest-cost drugs for negotiation: those whose cost to a patient exceeds the annual out-of-pocket threshold, the 40 drugs with the highest total Part D spending, the 40 drugs costing at least $10,000 per beneficiary per year, and the 20 drugs with the fastest-rising unit costs.

If negotiation fails, the price falls back to the lowest of the VA contract price, the average price across the ten largest OECD countries with per-capita income at least half of the U.S., or Medicaid 'best price'.

Requires manufacturers to pay Medicaid-style rebates for drugs dispensed to low-income ('rebate eligible') Part D enrollees, with rebates deposited into the Medicare Prescription Drug Account; manufacturers that refuse to sign a rebate agreement cannot have their drugs count as covered Part D drugs.

Requires the Secretary to set and apply a national formulary for Part D plans (including at least two drugs per category and class) and gives enrollees a process to request coverage of drugs not on the formulary or subject to prior authorization, step therapy, or tiered pricing.
Makes it easier for beneficiaries and their pharmacies to obtain coverage determinations by treating a prescription presented at a participating pharmacy as a request for a coverage determination.

Requires the Secretary to publicly explain the outcome of each negotiated price, and directs MedPAC to study and report to Congress on how the negotiations affect drug prices for beneficiaries, the federal government, states, plans, and the private market.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would face negotiated prices and rebate obligations for the first time in Medicare, and would bear the cost of lower prices. Medicare drug plans would lose sole control over formulary design.

drawbacks.text: Government negotiation may deliver smaller savings than advocates expect: Part D plans and their pharmacy benefit managers already negotiate aggressively with manufacturers, so added federal bargaining can produce only incremental savings beyond what private intermediaries extract.

The international reference-price fallback — pegging U.S. Medicare prices to those in ten foreign countries — could slow the U.S. launch or availability of some medicines if manufacturers respond by raising prices or delaying entry elsewhere, a trade-off between lower prices and access to new drugs.

The national formulary would shift significant coverage decisions from private plans to the Secretary of HHS, reducing plan flexibility to design cost-sharing that some beneficiaries prefer, though the bill preserves plans' ability to negotiate even deeper discounts and requires a beneficiary appeal process for off-formulary drugs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets the right place — the small number of extremely expensive, fast-rising drugs that drive Part D spending — and pairs price negotiation with concrete help for the low-income enrollees who face the worst costs. The savings depend on how hard the Secretary negotiates and may be modest where plans already bargain, and foreign reference pricing carries real access risks for new drugs. On balance the benefits to seniors and taxpayers outweigh the drawbacks, though the design leaves room for the process to underdeliver.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in October 2017, referred to two House committees and a health subcommittee the next day, and no committee ever acted on it before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Elijah Cummings introduced the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Act on October 26, 2017, joined by 17 original cosponsors.
The bill attracted 21 cosponsors in total, all Democrats.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction.
One day later, on October 27, 2017, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was ever recorded for the bill in the 115th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers are better off: the current system, in which Medicare is barred from negotiating and private plans negotiate rebates on the drugmakers' terms, remained intact. The Republican committee chairs faced no recorded vote on the issue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept the status quo

for.name: Elijah E. Cummings
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-MD), lead sponsor; senior member of the House Oversight Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 17 original cosponsors from his party.

for.name: 21 House Democratic cosponsors
for.role: Progressive-to-moderate Democrats including Lloyd Doggett, Peter Welch, Mark Pocan, Pramila Jayapal, Beto O'Rourke, and Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, which drew no Republican support.

against.name: Greg Walden
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Committee received the referral and never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill, which sat in its Health Subcommittee from October 2017 onward.

against.name: Kevin Brady
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Committee received the referral for provisions in its jurisdiction and took no recorded action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 sponsors — the lead sponsor plus 21 cosponsors — were Democrats, and the bill sat untouched in committees controlled by the Republican majority, which took no recorded action; no roll-call vote ever occurred.

industries.note: The bill would force them to negotiate prices with HHS for the highest-cost Part D drugs, accept a fallback price benchmarked to VA, foreign, and Medicaid 'best' prices if talks fail, and pay Medicaid-style rebates on drugs dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees. Those costs come directly out of the industry's pricing power, which is what keeps U.S. drug prices the highest in the world.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D plans and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Plans would lose sole authority over formulary design, which is the core of their negotiating leverage, and would have to use a Secretary-set formulary. But they would purchase drugs at negotiated prices and keep freedom to bargain for even deeper discounts.

The bill treats a prescription presented at a participating pharmacy as a request for a coverage determination, letting pharmacists trigger prior-authorization and step-therapy reviews directly on behalf of patients — a modest administrative easing for pharmacies and beneficiaries alike.
